transcript:
Header: 2026-10-06 14:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (Northpoint CTO), Sana (ML), Ethan (Infra), Jordan (Redwood SE)

(00:00) Alex Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we have the benchmark deck and raw logs ready, want to walk through the highlights and then go into tuning notes. Marcus, you good to start?

(00:12) Marcus Lee: Yeah thanks Alex. Appreciate the cadence. We've been really focused on p95 tail for our latency SLOs, and last week's baseline from OtherCloud showed p95 ~520ms for 512-token context. Curious to see Redwood numbers.

(00:26) Priya Nair: Great, so we ran the Redwood Dedicated profile with two model variants — the 13B open-arch quantized to 8-bit and the float16 baseline. We measured with the same request distribution you provided. Quick caveat: there's some network jitter on your side during provider runs, we saw spikes.

(00:43) (00:45) Sana Patel: Sorry interject, when you say "jitter" — is that on our VPC side or between Redwood and the baseline?

(00:48) Priya Nair: From packet captures and timestamps, it's mostly egress throttling at the baseline provider region during peak — some retransmits. On Redwood runs we saw much more consistent network times.

(01:05) Jordan Kim: To add, our benchmark harness pins concurrency and measures cold vs warm KV cache. Important to note: baseline runs often didn't account for KV warmup, so their cold-start p95 is inflated relative to steady-state.

(01:22) Ethan Rogers: That's exactly one of our concerns — production has lots of infrequent users and we do hit cold prefixes. How does Redwood handle prefix caching warmups?

(01:30) Priya Nair: Redwood's serving runtime keeps per-model KV cache and does prefix caching across requests; in these tests we simulated a 30-minute idle period and then a 1K user burst. The cold p95 was ~1.1s on 8-bit but warm steady-state p95 came down to ~210ms for the float16 runs, and ~260ms for 8-bit.

(02:00) Alex Martinez: To put that against your baseline: you said 520ms p95 — that's likely their average including cold starts and network variability. Our steady-state numbers are consistently lower, but we want apples-to-apples. We included runs where we forced cold starts for both platforms — results in the sheet.

(02:25) Marcus Lee: Right — the fairness thing. The sheet you shared had columns for cold/warm, concurrency, and tokens — I like that. But what about throughput under batching? If we increase batching, we need to keep tail latency bounded.

(02:40) Priya Nair: We tested batching policies: small batch (size 1-4) gave the best p95 under tight SLOs; larger batch improves tokens/sec but p95 tail rises — for the 13B 8-bit config, at batch size 8 we saw throughput increase ~1.9x but p95 moved from 260ms to ~480ms. For float16, batch 8 had p95 ~360ms.

(03:15) Sana Patel: That's interesting. What's the cost delta between float16 and 8-bit after batching?

(03:20) Jordan Kim: Rough numbers in the cost column: 8-bit reduces per-token GPU compute by ~35% in our runs, which maps to ~28% lower estimated infra cost when holding throughput constant. There's also memory and instance sizing benefits. But quality delta for some long-tail prompts — we flagged about 4% higher failure rate (response hallucination or truncation) on the 8-bit in the sample set.

(03:51) Marcus Lee: 4% is potentially material for us. We have a regulatory audit coming Q1 so we need to be conservative. Can you re-run with a more conservative quantization config?

(04:02) Priya Nair: Absolutely, we're proposing a mid-point quant config — it's not fully 8-bit across all kernels, it's mixed-precision; that tends to recover most quality while still saving ~18% cost. I'll run that and post results.

(04:20) Alex Martinez: Also worth noting — Redwood supports automatic fallback policies: if quality drops on a certain prompt pattern, we can route that pattern to float16 instances automatically. That gives you the cost upside globally while maintaining quality for sensitive paths.

(04:36) Rajiv Menon: How deterministic is the routing? We need audit trails for the fallback decisions.

(04:42) Maya Gomez: We log routing events and tie them to request ids; audit log contains model variant, route, timestamp. We can share sample logs (redacted).

(04:54) Marcus Lee: Good. Back to the baseline comparison — can you summarize where Redwood materially outperformed the baseline provider?

(05:01) Priya Nair: Sure. Three things: steady-state p50/p95 latency (Redwood ~95ms/210–260ms depending on precision vs baseline ~120/520ms), throughput under constrained concurrency (Redwood sustained higher req/s due to better batching and KV cache reuse), and consistency — less variance in tail latency. The baseline had higher variance largely due to network/egress and lack of persistent KV across workers.

(05:33) Ethan Rogers: Any specifics on the hardware used? We want to align instance types for fairness.

(05:38) Jordan Kim: Test runs used A100-equivalent GPU instances in both environments where possible. Baseline provider had slightly older drivers — we noted that as a confounder. We included an appendix with exact instance names, drivers, CUDA versions.

(05:55) Sana Patel: You mentioned KV cold-start p95 was 1.1s for 8-bit — that's pretty high. Does Redwood have warm pools to avoid that?

(06:02) Priya Nair: Yes, Dedicated can keep warm pools and configurable keep-alive policies. For the POC we left aggressive scale-down to simulate cost-aware autoscale; if you lock a minimal pool you can avoid that cold latency but incur baseline cost. We can model the cost tradeoff in the spreadsheet.

(06:25) Marcus Lee: Cool. On the quality side, can you show us where 8-bit misses? Any concrete examples?

(06:33) Priya Nair: We pulled 12 examples — long legal-style prompts and multi-step reasoning sequences showed the most deltas. I'll paste two redacted examples into the sheet. But remember these are model-sensitive; sometimes prompt engineering recovers behavior as well.

(06:51) Alex Martinez: Quick interruption — Sana, do you want to run a quick local test on one of those prompts during this call?

(06:56) Sana Patel: I can, give me a sec — ok running on a small subset against our baseline now. (typing noises) Hmm, for this one the baseline returned a truncated justification while Redwood float16 returned full justification; 8-bit trimmed a paragraph.

(07:20) Jordan Kim: That matches our flagged patterns. For those, one option is to use dynamic precision: switch to float16 for prompts with multi-step planning token counts over X. We can instrument that in route rules.

(07:36) Rajiv Menon: This dynamic switching — does it add routing latency?

(07:40) Priya Nair: Negligible — the routing decision is deterministic and metadata-based, most of the cost is the model compute time, switching at request time adds under 5ms overhead.

(07:52) Marcus Lee: Okay useful. Now on throughput — at peak we saw the baseline saturate at 90 req/s with rising tail, while Redwood sustained 150 req/s in the same profile. Is that accurate?

(08:02) Jordan Kim: For that specific test profile yes. The main reasons were continuous batching and higher packing efficiency on Redwood. Also the baseline instances were autoscaling slower which caused queuing.

(08:16) Ethan Rogers: Autoscale behavior — can we tune that in Redwood to match our cost targets? We want to avoid overprovisioning but also keep SLO.

(08:23) Priya Nair: Absolutely. In Dedicated you can set min capacity and two autoscale policies: latency SLO-based and utilization-based. We can propose a configuration that keeps a small warm pool plus fast-burst capacity. We'll include recommended policy in the follow-up doc.

(08:38) Alex Martinez: Also, we ran a sensitivity analysis on sequence length — p95 grows roughly linearly beyond 512 tokens; we included graphs. For your use-case where median tokens are 180 but some tails go to 1200, we recommend route-level limits and chunking for very long contexts.

(08:58) Sana Patel: Chunking is an app change; can Redwood do server-side context windowing?

(09:03) Priya Nair: We have primitives for partial context and stateful sessions you can use to stitch results. It often requires engineering work on the client but we can help with patterns.

(09:18) Marcus Lee: Let's talk about the comparison methodology — are the timestamps synchronized? We worried about clock skew between systems affecting p95 comparisons.

(09:26) Jordan Kim: We used NTP-synced test runners and included request/response timestamps from both client and server. For the baseline runs we also included tracer captures — the variance remained even after correcting for skew. See appendix B of the sheet.

(09:42) Rajiv Menon: One more question: security/compliance for Dedicated — do you provide SOC2 docs and can we see key management options?

(09:50) Maya Gomez: Yes, Redwood Dedicated offers KMS integrations and we shared our SOC2 and ISO certs earlier in the drive link. We'll re-send the security pack after this call.

(10:02) Marcus Lee: Perfect. On the procurement side, timeline — we're aiming for a decision by early Nov. Any blockers you expect?

(10:09) Alex Martinez: Main blockers: quality regression signal for 8-bit (we'll mitigate with mixed precision + routing), your network egress constraints for baseline parity, and the audit docs which we've already shared. With the runs we're scheduling we should be on track for early Nov.

(10:25) Priya Nair: OK next technical note — we saw one outlier where p99 spiked to 2.3s on Redwood 8-bit config; digging in, it was a GC pause on the runtime host during a log snapshot. We flagged it and that specific host was retired in the next run; no recurrence.

(10:40) Ethan Rogers: Good to know. Any other anomalies?

(10:43) Priya Nair: Baseline provider had intermittent API rate-limiting that caused retries which inflated p95. We removed the throttled samples for fairness and also show raw vs filtered numbers in the CSV.

(10:58) Marcus Lee: Alright, let's capture concrete deliverables — Alex, can you outline what you'll send after this call?

(11:04) Alex Martinez: Yes — I'll share the raw benchmark CSV, S3 link to logs, the updated sheet with mixed-precision runs and cost model, and a short note on recommended autoscale policy. Priya will add the quantization configs and flag the 12 long-tail prompts in the sheet.

(11:18) Marcus Lee: And we'll provide the long-tail prompt set and confirm a time for the networking deep-dive.

(11:25) Alex Martinez: Great. Any final questions?

(11:29) Sana Patel: One ask — can you include an expected Rx for quality delta as a function of prompt length? Even a heuristic table helps us decide which paths to route to float16.

(11:36) Priya Nair: Yes, we'll include a heuristic table and thresholds for dynamic routing.

(11:42) Alex Martinez: Thanks everyone — we'll post the artifacts and follow up on the action items.

(11:45) (call ends)
